sweep_summary: Kinyarwanda is in the catalog as 'tonal' (tonal-OR-pitch accent), decided from Kimenyi's undated web overview. this search of works with stress in the title listed 8 title hits (7 distinct works; Nsanzabiga appears twice). Read: Goldsmith & Mpiranya 2011 (already held by the project) — tone language with privative H on moras, abstract L-to-R quantity-sensitive moraic trochees used only to place verbal H tones, no stress claim; confirms and refines the tonal coding but does not supersede the deciding source. Read as abstract only: Nsanzabiga 1988 Nice thesis (SUDOC résumé) — the Rushobyo variety has shifted from tone to a free accent (first infix / antepenult / final) tending to fixed antepenultimate accent, contrasted with tonal standard Kinyarwanda; year fixed to 1988 (NNT 1988NICE2007) and the two Glottolog entries are one work. Philippson 1991 Paris V thesis: abstract read on theses.fr (tone-vs-penultimate-accent typology of East Bantu), no full text anywhere open. Not obtainable: Kimenyi 2002 Mellen tonal grammar (print; high priority), Furere & Rialland 1985 Benjamins chapter (paywalled DOI 10.1075/ssls.6.07fur, pp. 99-166; high priority as the fullest 'tons et accents' analysis), Furere & Rialland 1983 Foris (print; medium), Dubnova 1975 Russian article (print; low). Bonus open source Hyman 2009 confirms that Kinyarwanda penultimate lengthening is phonetic (after Myers 2005). Nothing read contradicts the catalog.archive. work done through Glottolog, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, HAL, theses.fr, SUDOC and HathiTrust APIs.

new_statements.quote: "There is a leftward shift of High tone in some cases that appears to be rhythmically motivated. If we group moras into groups of two from left to right, then it is natural to label one as strong and one as weak, even if the choice is a bit arbitrary. We label these feet as trochees (Strong-Weak). H root shifts leftward to a Strong position; H post shifts leftward to a Weak position ... We interpret this as an expression of quantitity-sensitivity in the accentual system: in particular, if the left-to-right assignment of metrical positions should encounter (so to speak) a long (i.e., two-mora) vowel in a Strong position, it treats the long vowel as comprising the strong position of the trochee"

new_statements.quote: Ainsi, il existe deux tons pertinents en kinyarwanda ; le ton haut et le ton bas. [1.3.3 L'OPPOSITION PHONOLOGIQUE TONALE] Deux tonèmes se sont dégagés de notre précédente étude. [...] Nous noterons phonologiquement le ton bas par un vide de signe diacritique et le ton haut par le signe / ´ / [...] Nous concluons que le ton haut et le ton bas sont des tonèmes. [1.3.4.1 La définition] Il est question ici des tons lexicaux. /´/ est haut et ponctuel / / est bas et ponctuel. || p. 58: En effet, la longueur vocalique phonologique en kinyarwanda est de type géminée. Il existera ainsi deux tons ponctuels BB, HB ou BH, associés à la forme VV. Dans ce cas, les tons s'associent aux mores et non aux syllabes.
new_statements.translation: Thus there are two relevant tones in Kinyarwanda: the high tone and the low tone. [1.3.3 The phonological tonal opposition] Two tonemes emerged from our preceding study. [...] We will note the low tone phonologically by the absence of a diacritic and the high tone by the sign / ´ / [...] We conclude that the high tone and the low tone are tonemes. [1.3.4.1 Definition] We are dealing here with lexical tones. /´/ is high and punctual; / / is low and punctual. || p. 58: Indeed, phonological vowel length in Kinyarwanda is of the geminate type. There will thus be two punctual tones LL, HL or LH associated with the form VV. In this case, tones associate to moras and not to syllables.

new_statements.relation_note: Confirms the catalog's tonal coding and Goldsmith & Mpiranya's mora-based tone description (tones associate with moras; long vowels bimoraic); it differs from them only analytically (two tonemes H/L vs. their privative H/toneless), which is immaterial to stress. It states no stress rule, so it adds nothing to the empty 'rule' field beyond confirming that a native-speaker phonological description of standard Kinyarwanda treats the word entirely in terms of tone.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kinyarwanda is described as a two-toneme language (lexical H vs. L, both level/'punctual'; a phonetic mid tone is an allophone of H, e.g. H lowered to mid at a word-initial vowel; tones dock on moras, long vowels are bimoraic and can carry LL, HL or LH). The thesis nowhere mentions stress or accent: 'accent' occurs 0 times in the text (fuzzy variants also 0), 'prosodie' only in the remark that the orthography ignores prosody, and 'intensité' only for vowel length. One distributional restriction is noted (p. 59): a high tone never appears on the first two syllables of trisyllables of shape VCVC(C)(C)V nor on the first syllable of CVC(C)VC(C)V; this is a tone-placement fact, not stress.
new_statements.exceptions: none relevant to stress; tonal rules only (H lowering to mid word-initially with rightward spread, sec. 1.3.2; L insertion on the second mora of an allophonically lengthened vowel, rule R10, p. 48)
new_statements.identity_note: Mpayimana 2003 describes standard Kinyarwanda from the author's own (Rwandan native-speaker) corpus; no dialect is singled out. Philippson 1991 is a comparative survey of ~50 East African Bantu languages in which Kinyarwanda is one sample language; its abstract names only Kikuyu and Swahili. Hoffman 1991 is a cross-Bantu syntax thesis, not a Kinyarwanda description.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's 'tonal' coding (Kimenyi web article; Goldsmith & Mpiranya 2011; Mpayimana 2003; Hoffman 1991) and adds an explicit typological classification from a comparative specialist: Rwanda-Rundi is 'langue tonale', 'not an accent language by our definition', with the penult relevant only as the landing site of a retracted final H. the compilers had only the theses.fr abstract; the full text is now read. Note Philippson treats 'rwanda/rundi' (Guthrie D61/D62, his group II 'Hautes terres de l'ouest') together, with Rwanda examples drawn from Coupez 1980, Kimenyi and Furere & Rialland 1983.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kinyarwanda (with Kirundi) is classed as a tone language, explicitly not an accent (stress) language in Philippson's typology (accent language = at most one H/culminative syllable per word): bisyllabic noun stems contrast three (short-vowel) or five (long-vowel) lexical tone patterns, Meeussen's rule applies systematically, every H is anticipated onto the preceding mora post-lexically, a word-final H retracts onto a long penult before pause, and a word-initial H shifts one mora rightward. No word stress is posited; the penult has no accentual status beyond hosting the retracted final H. Diachronically the language is placed at 'stage II', in transition toward but not yet an accentual system.
new_statements.exceptions: The rare fifth tone pattern (-cv:c&v type, e.g. rundi mahweerá) escapes final-H retraction; some Rwanda speakers insert a downstep between two H sequences (after Coupez 1980); dialectal variation between Rwanda and Rundi in the treatment of -cvcv́ stems (Rundi delinks the final H entirely).
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson treats 'rwanda' (Kinyarwanda, Guthrie D61 = JD61, his group II 'Hautes terres de l'ouest') jointly with Kirundi as 'rwanda/rundi', flagging the points where the two differ (final-H delinking in Rundi); his Rwanda data come from Coupez 1980, Kimenyi (1976, 1979, 1989) and Furere & Rialland 1983, i.e. standard Kinyarwanda. The other three works are about standard Kinyarwanda per their titles.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The thesis is a syntactic study (causatives, applicatives, double-object constructions) with no phonology, prosody or accent section; its only prosodic content for Kinyarwanda is a transcription convention borrowed from Kimenyi (1980) marking high and falling tone with low tone unmarked (p. 10 fn. 3), plus a footnote that relativization 'is marked by a high tone on the verb rather than by a separate morpheme' (p. 217 fn. 12). It treats Kinyarwanda as a tone language and says nothing at all about word stress, accent placement or prominence: the scanned of all 245 pages has 0 occurrences of 'stress', 'accent', 'prominen', 'penult', 'prosod', 'pitch' or 'intonation'.
new_statements.identity_note: Hoffman's Kinyarwanda data are taken from Kimenyi (1980), A relational grammar of Kinyarwanda (standard Rwandan Kinyarwanda); the thesis also treats Chichewa, SiSwati, Sesotho, Chi-Mwi:ni, KiMeru and non-Bantu languages, but the quoted footnote is specifically about Kinyarwanda.

sources.note: First-hand (co-author Mpiranya is a native speaker). Treats Kinyarwanda as a tone language with a privative High vs. toneless contrast on moras (point 3: 'Low toned' roots 'are best analyzed as bearing no tone'); posits abstract moraic trochees built left-to-right from the word edge, quantity-sensitive, whose only function is to locate shifted verbal H tones. Never claims phonetic or phonological word stress. Confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding and refines it with the metrical detail (L-to-R binary moraic feet, quantity-sensitive).

sources.quote: theses.fr abstract (direct download summary, not verbatim): the thesis surveys the prosodic systems of ~30 East African Bantu languages from fully tonal (Kikuyu) to penultimate demarcative-accent (Swahili), analysing tone displacement/anticipation and proposing that the emergence of a penultimate demarcative accent drove the systems' evolution.
sources.note: Comparative thesis covering Kinyarwanda [kin] among ~50 East Bantu languages (Glottolog language code list); it would classify Kinyarwanda on the tone-vs-penultimate-accent continuum but the abstract does not single it out. No open text: theses.fr gives no PDF, HAL author search (13 Philippson deposits) has no thesis, HathiTrust OCLC lookup empty. Glottolog's private 'hh' collection holds a scan (fn field) but it is not public. Not previously in our bibliography.

sources.quote: Hypothesis that Kirundi and Kinyarwanda tonal systems developed through 'the incursion into these languages of a rhythmic pattern of alternating strong and weak syllable positions' driving rules that 'shifted High tones one mora to the left or right in order to associate a High tone with a metrically strong position'. Again rhythm conditions tone placement; the languages are described as tonal.
